planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and set transplants out only once nights stay reliably warm, since this long-season pepper needs a full hot summer to size up.

directions: This curved, elongated pod takes its name (goat's horn) from its shape and is a traditional landrace of south-central Chile's Araucanía and Biobío regions, grown chiefly by Mapuche and campesino farmers for drying and smoking. Pick pods as they ripen to deep red, then smoke them slowly over wood coals before grinding to produce the toasted, smoky base of merkén, Chile's signature Mapuche spice blend. The plant is a prolific, medium-height bush best grown in full sun with steady moisture through fruit set, and it tolerates the warm, dry summers of its home valleys well. Fresh pods also work in sauces and pickles, but the variety's reputation rests on its performance once dried and smoked.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste
Universidad de Chile agronomy extension publications on Mapuche merkén

planting.note: Direct-sow after the soil has warmed past 65F, since cold, wet soil rots the seed before it can germinate.

directions: Tórtola takes its name from the mottled grey-and-brown speckling on its seed coat, said to resemble the plumage of the eared dove (tórtola) common across central Chile's farmland. It is a traditional bush-type dry bean of the Chilean central valley, grown for both the fresh shell stage used in porotos granados, a classic summer stew of fresh beans, corn, and squash, and for the dried bean used in winter soups. Grow it like any bush bean, direct-sown in full sun with even watering through flowering and pod fill, and either harvest young pods green-shelled for granados or leave pods to dry fully on the plant for storage beans. It is a workhorse home-garden variety rather than a market crop, kept going mostly through seed-saving within families.
sources: INIA Chile bean germplasm collection (Banco Base de Semillas)
Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste
Chilean home-garden seed-saving networks (Red de Semillas Libres de Chile)

planting.note: Direct-sow in hills or mounds after the soil is warm, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room to run.

directions: Named camote (sweet potato) for its elongated, tapered, tan-and-orange rind that mimics a giant sweet potato, this is one of the everyday zapallo squashes sold by the slice in Chilean produce markets. The dense, deep-orange flesh is sweeter and firmer than many Cucurbita maxima types, and it is the squash of choice for pastel de zapallo, sopaipillas worked with mashed squash into the dough, and the squash cubes simmered into cazuela. Give the sprawling vines full sun, rich soil, and steady water through fruit set, then cure harvested fruit in a warm spot for a couple of weeks to concentrate sweetness and extend storage. It stores well into winter, which is part of why it remains a staple squash in central Chilean home gardens and markets alike.
sources: Instituto Nacional de Desarrollo Agropecuario (INDAP) Chile crop guides

planting.note: Direct-sow in blocks rather than single rows for reliable wind pollination, after the danger of frost has fully passed.

directions: Curagua is a traditional popcorn-type maize landrace grown for centuries in the coastal and central valleys of Chile, long predating European contact, and it is still planted by smallholder farmers to make cabritas or palomitas, Chile's version of popcorn, as well as toasted ground meal. Its small, hard, pointed kernels pop reliably when dried fully and stored, distinguishing it from the soft dent and flour corns more common in modern Chilean fields. Grow it like other open-pollinated corn, in blocks for pollination, full sun, and consistent moisture during tasseling and ear fill, then let ears dry fully in the husk before shelling and curing kernels for popping. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it from other corn varieties if you intend to save true seed.
sources: Universidad de Chile Facultad de Ciencias Agronómicas maize landrace studies
Red de Semillas Libres de Chile

planting.note: Direct-sow once soil has warmed, providing a trellis if growing the pole-type strain rather than the bush form.

directions: Coscorrón is a plump, kidney-shaped Chilean heirloom bean with a cream background mottled in maroon-red, grown in the central valley and parts of Chiloé alongside other traditional poroto landraces. Its large seed size and good flavor make it a favorite for porotos granados and the thick bean-and-squash stews served through the Chilean summer and fall, as well as for simple winter bean soups once dried. Treat it as a standard warm-season bean, direct-sown after frost danger passes, watered evenly through flowering and pod fill, and either picked young for fresh shelling or left to dry fully on the vine for storage. It survives today mostly through small-scale farmers and home gardeners who save and replant their own seed each year.
sources: INIA Chile bean germplasm collection (Banco Base de Semillas)
Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste
Red de Semillas Libres de Chile
